The case of Timothy Masters stands as one of the most significant wrongful conviction sagas in Colorado's legal history, raising fundamental questions about prosecutorial conduct, forensic evidence standards, and the mechanisms meant to prevent miscarriages of justice.

"The people of this community — and the family of Peggy Hettrick — deserve to know that whoever is responsible for this crime is held accountable, and that requires an unbiased review free from any conflict of interest."

## A Case That Raised Broader Questions

Legal experts say the Masters case has become a cautionary tale about the dangers of relying on behavioral profiling in the absence of physical evidence, as well as the consequences of prosecutorial discovery failures.

"This case really shines a light on how psychological theories, when treated as science in a courtroom, can lead to wrongful convictions," said one criminal justice professor who has followed the case closely. "It's a warning sign for how these cases are built and tried."

The Colorado attorney general's office previously conducted a review of the original investigation and prosecution, though the full findings of that review — and the extent of any misconduct — remain subjects of ongoing debate and, in some cases, litigation.

## What's Next

With Masters now free and his name cleared, attention turns to whether the newly identified suspect will face charges. A special prosecutor, once appointed, will be tasked with reviewing the DNA evidence, original case files, and any new investigative leads before deciding how to proceed.

Hettrick's family, meanwhile, has waited more than two decades for answers.

"We just want to know what really happened to Peggy," a family member said outside the courthouse. "We want justice — real justice, for her."

Masters has not ruled out pursuing a civil claim against Larimer County and the city of Fort Collins over his prosecution and imprisonment, according to people close to his legal team. For now, though, his attorneys say he is simply trying to adjust to life after 9 1/2 years behind bars for a crime he did not commit.

CNN will continue to follow developments in this case as the special prosecutor review moves forward.
